description: Team consisting of City of Kamloops employees and additional members.
summary: The Kamloops Burning Activity Calendar is a web app that harmonizes NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots from MODIS and VIIRS into one record for Kamloops and the Southern Interior of British Columbia, from November 2000 to today. The two sensor families cannot simply be added together: VIIRS detects about 8.6 times as many hotspots per satellite as MODIS, and the number of satellites has changed five times. The app counts hotspots per satellite, converts the MODIS years to VIIRS units with a factor measured while both flew, and ranks each month and each summer against the same period in other years. A fire manager, scientist or land manager picks an area and sees whether burning is below, near or above normal for the time of year, explores 26 years as a calendar heat map, a timelapse map and a 3D view that outlines where large fires burned, and downloads the hotspots and the monthly index. It runs from cached data with no live connection.
details:
What it does

The app opens on the Kamloops area and says in one sentence how the current month compares with the same month in other years, with its index, rank and typical value. A calendar heat map shows every month since November 2000, coloured by hotspot activity or by how far the month is from normal, with a Summer column that rates June to September as a whole. Other views show the season building up day by day, a map of the hotspots, a timelapse, and a 3D view in which columns rise where fires burn and an outline stays for 12 months around each large burnt patch. A user can switch between preset areas of the Southern Interior, enter a box, or circle a region on the map to get that region's own calendar. The hotspots and the monthly index download as CSV.

How the records are harmonized

Step 1, count per satellite. Each month's hotspots are divided by the number of satellite-days in service, leaving out outage days and days with no scene in NASA's granule catalogue, so that more satellites do not look like more fire.

Step 2, one unit. From February 2012 the index is the VIIRS rate. Before that it is the MODIS rate times 8.6, a factor measured over 2012 to 2021, when both sensors flew and the MODIS orbits were still steady. The years 2022 to 2025 are kept to check the factor on data it was not fitted on.

Step 3, rank, not count. Each month is ranked against the same calendar month in other years and put in one of five classes, from much below normal to much above normal. Each summer is ranked the same way against the other summers.

Months are counted in local Pacific time, low-confidence detections are dropped, and one fixed industrial heat source near Kamloops is removed before any scaling.

What was tested and what to keep in mind

Hotspots are detections, not hectares burned. Values before February 2012 are scaled from MODIS and are good to about a factor of 2: the order of the years is better supported than their level. Compared with British Columbia's records of area burned, the index puts the years 2003 to 2025 in nearly the same order (rank correlation 0.88). Small areas have too few hotspots to rank single months, so the app says so and rates the whole summer instead. The newest months use provisional near-real-time data and are marked.

Why it matters

Fire managers, scientists and land managers get one consistent 26-year picture from sensors that cannot be compared directly, and can see at a glance whether a month or a summer is unusual for their area. In the Kamloops area, 2003, 2021 and 2023 stand far above every other summer in the record.

Tools

Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, Plotly and SQLite. The terrain under the maps comes from NASA GIBS. Automated tests recompute the app's numbers from the data by a second route.

Use of AI tools

AI assistants (Claude, through Claude Code, and a Cursor agent) were used under the team's direction for research and source gathering, data analysis, writing the code and its tests, documentation and drafting this description. The app itself has no AI or machine-learning component. The choice of harmonization method is the team's.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS active fire hotspots: MODIS and VIIRS 375 m (yearly country files)
NASA FIRMS API: near-real-time and recent hotspots
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services): terrain under the maps and the MODIS land and water mask
NASA Earthdata CMR granule search: days with no satellite scene
projectRefs: ASTER Global Digital Elevation Model (NASA and METI, Japan), served through NASA GIBS
BC Wildfire Service historical fire incident locations (Open Government Licence, British Columbia): check against area burned
